rv.q: For better or worse — and for me shows this cathartic are only for the better — we’re home.
Nonetheless, the takeaway is that this show (a finalist for the Pulitzer) could be staged on the back of a truck and still break your heart.
It’s the best use of this often awkward space I’ve ever seen — or, rather, felt.
Rarely do you find a funeral home you’re unhappy to leave.
Cerveris, whose performance is deeply disturbing in all the right ways, shows you a man acting out constantly, a man whose denial of self has meant excessive hunger for stimuli of all kinds.

Surrounded by audiences, this 1 hour 40 minute nonstop treasure of invention retains the unpretentious chamber-musical feel of director Sam Gold's masterly production, while scenes from Bechdel's story rise and disappear into the floor like slippery memories on David Zinn's ingenious set.
For anyone who cares about adventurous musical theater, it's not to be missed.
Fun Home is a marvelous achievement, full of humor as well as rue.
This is a show that manages to be both heartbreaking and heartwarming, often simultaneously.

There’s only one lyric at the beginning to clue us in: “But now I’m the one who’s 43/ and stuck/ I can’t find my way through.” Was 43 the age of her father at his death? And will the cartoon be her solvent? A couple of lines in the libretto would go a long way to making the piece feel more purposeful.
Fun Home is a small musical with a big heart, one that finds profound meaning in quiet moments.

"Composer Jeanine Tesori and book writer/lyricist Lisa Kron tackle the material with great sensitivity and warmth. Their adaptation boasts a solid chamber-pop score, a handful of wonderful scenes and a winning cast.“Fun Home” has a lot going for it, thanks to the great affection and humor it accords its flawed, searching characters.
Fun Home is a transcendent experience.
“Fun Home” is a thoroughly dynamic piece that is just as emotionally piercing, good-humored and enjoyable as it is sharp, focused and culturally conscious.
"Alison Bechdel’s provocative tale has now been translated to the stage in the extremely ambitious, extremely moving musical 'Fun Home.
Fun Home is the best Broadway musical in years.

Writer and lyricist Lisa Kron ("Well") and composer Jeanine Tesori ("Caroline, or Change") turn this into an uplifting musical drama of rare intensity, honesty and beauty through melodically rich songs that summon yearning, heartache and joy.
On Broadway, where Fun Home opened Sunday at Circle in the Square, the show feels even more powerful, and more unsettling.
Fun Home manages to use an oft-unserious medium to deliver something seriously, singularly moving.
It remains the inventive, entertaining, in places exhilarating, and almost inexpressibly heartbreaking show I saw Off-Broadway at the Public Theater a couple of years ago.
Not an easy story to translate into a musical.
Absolutely fantastic in every way.
Fun Home is a special, special show.
Fun Home, a powerful, poignant musical not to be missed.
Fun Home is the rare musical that touches the heart, inspires the mind and makes the feet tap along to the music.
The message that love is love is one that we’ll gladly subject to long-run-itis.
The size and enthusiasm of the crowd tips off the buzz surrounding the musical since it premiered off-Broadway a year and a half ago.
While I found this more of a production to admire than enjoy, keen aficionados of edgy music theatre will most likely appreciate Fun Home.

There’s nothing really wrong with that, I suppose, but, like the fun house mirror, what I know to be a funny, moving, and endlessly smart story is reflected back at me as fairly average Broadway fare.

cn.t: Critics hail "Fun Home" as an extraordinary, blazingly original musical that brings fresh sophistication to Broadway. The adaptation of Alison Bechdel's memoir earns praise for its emotional depth, inventive staging, and heartbreaking power.

sg.ra: In the 3/4 thrust configuration these front rows put you at the lip of the playing area with actors entering from aisles directly beside you. Headout notes rows AA-B are 'closest to the stage' and audiences are 'roped into the play's action.' Because the stage is surrounded on three sides, the acting is deliberately blocked so no front row gets a sustained back-of-actor view, but individual moments will face away from you — that is inherent to in-the-round and not a flaw of this section.

Universally cited as the optimal vantage in this thrust venue — close enough to feel the intimacy of a 776-seat room with only 10 rows, but one row back from the front so sightlines catch the whole three-sided playing area. Headout: 'Center Orchestra - rows B, C and D' positioned centrally are 'possibly the best seats in the house.' The in-the-round blocking is designed so these central rows at eye-level with the floor see choreography and staging as intended.

Because the venue only has 10 rows total and stadium-inclined seating, rows H-I still feel close to the thrust while giving elevated sightlines that reveal staging patterns on the floor — useful for musicals with choreography. Headout: 'Rows H and I in the upper middle level offer a great view of the stage and the prices are lower than those of the premium orchestra seats.' AVFMS reviewer MusicaltheatreWhiz in H144 (Just in Time, Feb 2026): 'There really isn't a bad seat in the house!' TripAdvisor: 'up is better for musicals.'

In a typical Broadway house the last row would be a skip, but Circle in the Square is only 10 rows deep so row K is roughly where Row G would be in a standard theater. AVFMS danielb9 at K109 (Just in Time, Feb 28 2026): 'Enough legroom to be comfortable and despite being in the back row felt very connected to the action.' Multiple reviews note 'no obstruction' and 'great seat' for row K. Stadium incline ensures sightlines over heads. The in-the-round nature means some scenes still play toward the opposite side, but this is a venue property not a section flaw.

sg.n: Side Sections - Long Arms of the Horseshoe (100s & 200s)
sg.ra: The two long 'wide sides' of the horseshoe (the 100 and 200 numbered sections per BWW forum user Patash's question about 102/202 numbering) give a profile view of the main action. TripAdvisor: 'the two wide sides are fine' and are preferred over 'straight in front' which is 'too far from the rear end of the main stage.' AVFMS samr32 at C207 (Just in Time, Feb 26 2026): 'Amazing seat! Can see both stages so well, and the actors (including Jonathan Groff) run up and down the aisle right near you.' The 300-degree blocking means side sections regularly get face-forward moments; not behind-stage.

The one sustained warning across every source is the extreme corner seats where the horseshoe's ends meet the stage. Headout/TickPick specifically: 'seats 438-440 are obstructed when actors perform on the far left of the stage and vice versa for the opposite side' (437-439). Unlike the rest of the house where in-the-round angles are temporary, these corner positions can have whole extended scenes played entirely out of view on the opposite corner. In a 3/4 thrust with actors using the full perimeter, this is a structural flaw of the seat, not a temporary blocking issue.
